The result is a weepie musical with an uncheapened humanity you can almost touch. Lovely.
The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry is now a heart-warming musical starring Mark Addy that deserves to become an unlikely West End hit.

It feels like ridiculous whimsy. Harold, above, is wearing boat shoes, and has said nothing to his sad wife Maureen (Jenna Russell, deeply moving as the one left behind). A terrible tragedy has driven them apart.
It takes you on a journey that sends you home feeling a bit lighter, a bit more hopeful, than you did before.
We all should have been transported, but the ground underfoot is mushy.
It’s a bit cosy, but not entirely so – there’s a wildness and darkness bubbling beneath the surface that means The Unlikely Pilgrimage packs a surprising punch.

The truth, though, is that while the folk-inflected songs by Mike Rosenberg (known as Passenger) are amiable enough — Chris Poon’s compact band cut a dash and the lyrics inject some surprisingly salty humour at times — Joyce’s script is oddly underpowered. This is a show created, crafted and performed by consummate theatrical professionals all working hard to move and entertain the audience.
The recipe is nigh-on foolproof and I confess, I am as susceptible to its charms as the next man.
The wherewithal to keep going in the face of life’s myriad challenges is beautifully portrayed in this feelgood and inspiring production.
The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry is a rare beast: a musical that asks you to feel deeply without ever making you feel foolish for doing so.
Funny, affecting and tender, The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry is a production that unashamedly pulls on every emotion to touch the hardest of hearts.
Adapted for the stage by Rachel Joyce from her 2012 novel, with a brilliant score by Passenger, this new musical is a profoundly moving celebration of hope.
It has slipped gently into the audience’s hearts, and made itself entirely at home.

cn.t: Critics warmly embrace this gentle, heart-warming musical adaptation, praising Mark Addy's superb lead performance and the show's emotional resonance. The folk-infused score and thoughtful staging effectively capture Harold's redemptive journey.

vr.q: I am delighted to have a new British musical of this caliber open in the West End.
